title: Three Loud Things
author: written for Leo
blurb: Three stories about being told you are too much, and what is actually going on.

p: Rafi did not know he was doing it.

That was the part nobody believed. When Mrs Okafor said his name in the tired voice — not cross, which would have been easier, but tired — he would look up and find his own right hand still going on the desk without him, doing something quick with the fingers, the way a tap goes on dripping after you have turned it off.
He would stop it. He would sit on it. And four minutes later it would be back, and he would not have decided anything.
“Sorry,” he said, about eleven times a day.

Ari, who sat next to him and was his friend, said once, kindly, “Can you not, though?” and Rafi had said “yeah, sorry,” and had meant it completely, and had done it again before the end of the lesson. After that he stopped saying sorry out loud and started saying it inside instead, which took less time and made him feel worse.

By the middle of Year Three he had worked out something about himself, and it was this: there was a thing in him that came out wrong. Other people had the same amount of whatever it was and theirs stayed in. His got out, on desks, in corridors, and in his voice, which arrived in rooms slightly before he did.
He did not tell anybody he had worked this out. You do not go around saying that sort of thing.
On Thursdays he had drums.

Drums were in a small room behind the hall with carpet on the walls, and his teacher was called Wes, and Wes had hands like a bricklayer and a way of not filling up silences. Rafi had been going for two years. He could play things now that made Wes sit back on his stool and go quiet for a second and then say, “again.”
That Thursday, Wes said, “Mrs Okafor rang.”
Rafi's whole chest went cold. He put the sticks down on the snare, neatly, side by side, the way you do when you are about to be talked to.
“She says you're drumming on the desks.”
“I'll stop.”
“What are you playing?”
Rafi looked up.
“When you do it,” said Wes. “On the desk. What is it?”
“I don't — it's not anything. It's just tapping.”
“Do it.”
“What?”
“Do it now. The desk thing.” Wes pushed the practice pad across. “Go on.”
And Rafi put his hand on the pad, and his hand did nothing at all.

He tried. He genuinely tried, sitting there in the carpeted room with his ears going hot, and what came out was slow and lumpy and stupid, nothing like the thing that came out of him in maths when he was not looking, and after about fifteen seconds he stopped and said, “I can't.”
“No,” said Wes, and he sounded pleased about it, which made no sense. “Course you can't.”
“Why is that good?”
Wes leaned back and looked at the ceiling for a while.

“Because it means it isn't naughtiness,” he said. “Naughtiness you can do on purpose. That's the whole point of it.” He tapped the side of the snare twice with one finger. “What you've got is hands that are quicker than the rest of you. They find the beat in things before you've decided to look for it. The extractor fan out there is doing something in five, by the way. Has been all lesson.”
Rafi listened. It was. He had not noticed he had noticed.
“That's not a problem,” said Wes. “That's the job. The problem is the room.”
“I'm not allowed to be like this in the room.”
“You're not allowed to be LOUD in the room. Those are different sizes of thing, and I want you to hear the difference, because I think you've been carrying the big one around.”
Rafi did not say anything, because there was something happening in his throat.

“Here.” Wes dug about in the drawer under the shelf and came up with a square of grey foam, about the size of a phone, the sort they cut up for lining cases. He threw it over. “Pocket. It makes no noise at all. I've had mine since I was fourteen.”
“You still do it?”
“I'm doing it now,” said Wes. He was, too — left hand, down by his leg, something in seven. He had been the whole time.
“So it doesn't stop.”
“No.”
“Ever?”

“Not for me it hasn't.” Wes picked his sticks back up. “You're not too loud, Rafi. You're playing in a room where nobody else can hear the song. That's a room problem. You just have to be the one who remembers it, because they're not going to.”
Then he counted four, and they played, and it was extremely loud and completely allowed.

Rafi still forgets. He forgot twice the following Tuesday. But the foam is in his pocket on school days, and when Mrs Okafor says his name in the tired voice he does something now that he did not used to do, which is that he notices what his hand was playing before he stops it.
It was five, that time. The same as the fan.
Otis broke the window in the corridor by the art room, and it was an accident, and nobody believed that either.

It had been a ball, and it had not even been his ball, but it had been his foot, and the sound a window makes is a sound that brings adults from a long way away. By the time he was standing in the caretaker's room he had already run through what was coming and decided to get in first.
“It's fine,” he said. “I'm the bad one. Everyone knows.”
The caretaker was called Mr Iremonger and he was about a hundred years old and he was writing in a book.
“Mm,” he said.
“You can just ring my mum.”
“I will.” He went on writing.
Otis stood there with his hands hanging and waited to be told he was a disgrace, and it did not come, and after a while the waiting got worse than the telling would have been.
“What's the book?”

“Things that happened.” Mr Iremonger turned it round so Otis could see. The page said, in small grey handwriting: *Tues 14th. Corridor window, art room end, outer pane. Football. Boy uninjured. Glass swept, boarded, ordered.*
Otis read it twice.
“It doesn't say anything about me.”
“It says a boy.”
“It doesn't say I'm —” He stopped.
“Doesn't say you're what?”
Otis did not answer that.

Mr Iremonger turned back a page, and another, and Otis saw that the book went a long way. *Flood, boiler room, burst feed.* *Bird in the hall, released via fire door.* *Pane, lower gym, hail.* Dates going back and back. Hundreds of them. Years of things, in the same small grey hand, and not one of the entries said anybody was anything.
“Why don't you write it down properly?” said Otis. “Like — whose fault.”

“Because that's not what happened.” Mr Iremonger licked his thumb and turned another page. “What happened is a window went in. Fault is something people add on afterwards, mostly at children, and it isn't very useful for ordering glass.”
He said it without any weight at all, the way you would say the boiler needs bleeding.
“Am I in it a lot?”
That was out of Otis's mouth before he had permission from himself to ask it. His ears went hot.

Mr Iremonger did not answer straight away. He put on the other glasses, the ones on the string, and went back through the book properly, slowly, from the beginning of the year before, licking his thumb, and it took a while, and Otis stood there and thought he might actually be sick.
“Four,” he said.
“Four what?”

“Four times in two years. The tap you left on in the Year Two toilets. The chair leg. A window today. And you were in the bird one, but only because you opened the door, which I put in as a good thing and nobody ever asks about.”
“Four,” said Otis.
“Four.”

Otis stood very still. Because the number in his own head — the one he walked around with, the one that had made him say *I'm the bad one* before anyone else could — was not four. It was not anywhere near four. It was a great grey heap with no edges, and it had been getting bigger for two years, and now here it was written down in small grey handwriting with dates on it, and it fitted on one page, and there was an enormous amount of room left over.
“That's not very many,” he said.
“No,” said Mr Iremonger. “It's a school. Things go in.”
He closed the book and put it on the shelf with the others, and there were a lot of others.
“Does that mean I'm not —”

“It means a window went in on Tuesday,” said Mr Iremonger. “That's all it means. It's a fact about a window.” He looked at Otis over the top of the glasses. “You've been doing the other sort of adding-up, I think. It's very common and it's very inaccurate and I'd give it up.”
Otis's mum came, and was cross, and it was not a good evening. That part did not get fixed by anything.

But he thought about the page with all the room left on it for a long time afterwards, and something in him that had been quietly getting heavier for two years stopped getting heavier, which is not the same as getting lighter but is the thing that has to happen first.
His dad was in a mood, and Bram had been tracking it since the car.

He was extremely good at this. He could tell from the way the keys went down on the side — one sound if it was fine, another sound entirely if it was not — and today they had gone down in the second way, hard, and then there had been a long silence in the kitchen with the fridge humming in it.
So Bram ran the check. This is what he always did, and it took about four seconds, because he had got fast at it.

The homework was done. The bowl was in the dishwasher. He had not shouted at his sister since Sunday and that one had not even been properly his. He had left his bag in the hall, which was a possible, so he went and moved it, quietly, and stood it against the wall with the straps tucked in.

Then he sat on the stairs where you can hear the kitchen and could not think of anything else, which was the worst part, because if you cannot find it you cannot fix it, and it just goes on being in the house.
After a while his dad came out and said, “You all right?”
“Yeah.”
“You've gone quiet.”
“You've gone quiet,” said Bram.
His dad stopped in the hall with his hand on the bannister.
“Yeah,” he said. “I have. Sorry.”
He sat down on the stairs, which he had to do sideways because he did not really fit, and for a bit neither of them said anything.
“Is it me?”
“What?”
“Is it me,” said Bram. “The mood.”

And his dad did something Bram had not expected, which was that he did not say *no, of course not, don't be silly* in the quick voice that means yes a bit. He actually stopped and thought about it, and it took him a few seconds, and then he said:
“No. Not this one.”
“Really?”

“Really. This one is about a man called Peter Hannay, who you have never met, who did something today that has made a mess of about six weeks of my work, and I've got to sort it out and I don't know how yet.” He rubbed his face with both hands. “And I brought it in the house with me instead of leaving it in the car, which is my fault and not yours.”
Bram sat with this.
“I thought it was the bag.”
“The bag?”
“I left my bag in the hall. I moved it.”
His dad laughed, once, not in a mean way, and then stopped laughing quite quickly.
“How long have you been doing that?” he said.
Bram shrugged, because the answer was *always*, and *always* is hard to say out loud.

“Right,” said his dad. He was quiet again, but it was a different quiet. “OK. New rule. You're allowed to ask. Any time. Just say, is this one mine — and I'll tell you the truth, even if the truth is a bit yes.”
“What if it is a bit yes?”

“Then I'll say, a bit, and here's the bit, and we'll sort out the bit.” He nudged him with his elbow. “But most of them aren't yours, mate. Most of them come from a long way off. You've been standing out in weather that isn't even from your sky.”
They sat on the stairs a while longer.
“Is it going to be all right? The Peter Hannay thing?”
“Probably. Most things are. It's just going to be annoying for a fortnight.”
“OK,” said Bram.

He still checks. You do not stop doing a thing you have done for years because somebody explains it to you on a staircase. But he has asked the question four times since then, and three of those times the answer was no, and the fourth time his dad said *a bit — the shoes in the doorway* — and they moved the shoes, and that was the whole of it, and it turned out the bit was very small when you actually looked at it directly.
Which is generally true of bits, it turns out. It is the ones you never ask about that go on growing in the dark.
